summary: Describes how to register character sets with IANA. Many protocols, including MIME, can use many charsets, so a name for each charset is needed and an indication of whether it can be used in MIME text. It was replaced by RFC 2978.

eli5.summary: It is the process for giving a standard name to each way of encoding text, so programs agree on what they are reading.

subtitle: The process for registering character encodings with IANA.

tldr.problem: Many Internet protocols can use different character encodings. Without a standardized registry and naming process, implementations could not agree on what encoding a message uses.
tldr.mechanism: This BCP establishes a formal registration process: proposals are posted for community review, a designated charset reviewer evaluates them, and IANA records approved charsets in a registry and assigns each one a unique enumerated value.
tldr.outcome: The process ensures charsets are properly documented and labeled before use in Internet messages. It was updated by RFC 2978 with refinements to the procedure.

today: RFC 2278 is a Best Current Practice that was updated by RFC 2978, which provided refinements and corrections to the charset registration procedures. The basic process described here remains in use.

sections.title: What Is a Charset
sections.content:
A charset is a method of converting a sequence of octets (bytes) into a sequence of characters. The term evolved from the older "character set" because modern charsets do much more than just map bytes to characters—they can handle multi-byte sequences and even provide directionality information.

The definition distinguishes between three related concepts: a Coded Character Set (CCS) is an abstract mapping from characters to integers, a Character Encoding Scheme (CES) is a mapping from integers to octets, and a charset is the complete process from octets to characters. MIME and other modern protocols use charsets extensively, so each one must have a standardized name and be documented before use.
sections.eli5: A charset is like a dictionary that tells a computer how to turn numbers (the bytes it receives) into letters you can read. Different languages and systems use different dictionaries.

sections.title: Registration Requirements
sections.content:
To be registered, a charset must meet several requirements. It must be defined by a standards body or organization and must be fully specified in a stable, openly available document. The definition is not invented in the registration process itself; it must exist elsewhere first. Charsets intended for MIME must explicitly note whether they are suitable for use in MIME text objects.

Each charset must be assigned at least one name that conforms to MIME syntax rules. When multiple names are assigned, one is designated as the primary name and others are aliases. The names must uniquely identify the charset and must be suitable as MIME parameter values.
sections.eli5: A charset can only be registered if it is already documented somewhere official, has at least one standardized name, and works properly as a charset rather than something else like a transfer encoding.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
Registration begins with a public proposal posted to the ietf-charsets mailing list. The community has two weeks to review and comment on the charset definition and its proposed name. After the public comment period, the registration proposer submits the application to IANA and a designated charset reviewer, appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director.

The reviewer evaluates the application and makes a decision within 14 days. If the charset is controversial, the reviewer may conduct a last call to the full IETF. Once approved, IANA registers the charset, assigns it a unique MIBenum value (used in protocols like the Printer MIB), and makes the registration available to the community. A reviewer may also recommend standards-track processing if the specification warrants it.
sections.eli5: To register a new system, you announce it for two weeks and let people ask questions. A special reviewer checks it, and if it looks good, IANA writes it down and gives it a number.

sections.title: What Gets Registered
sections.content:
The registration template requires submitting the charset name (or names, if aliases are provided), and a reference to a published specification that fully describes the charset. The specification must accurately describe the encoding method, and if the charset is composed of a Coded Character Set and a Character Encoding Scheme, their definitions must either be included or clearly referenced.

Registered charset information is posted in the IANA registry file and included in the periodically updated IETF "Assigned Numbers" RFC. Some registrations are also published as separate Informational RFCs. The registration does not constitute endorsement or approval by the IANA or IETF, but rather a record that the charset exists and is formally documented.
sections.eli5: When you register a charset, you give it a name and point to the official rules for how it works. Then IANA puts it in a public list so other programs can find out about it.
